name: Aisha Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, absolutely. I'm Aisha, I'm 43, and I'm a junior on a building crew that puts up factory-made timber houses. I was a graphic designer for eighteen years before that, so I've been on site just under two years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The panels come on a lorry, whole walls with the windows already in, and we lift them with a crane and fix them together, then do the carpentry inside. My job is guiding panels in, fixing them off, sealing joints, and then trims and stairs, where I'm still slow. I love seeing a house go from a concrete slab to a shell in three days, it's like a drawing coming off the page. What wears me out is the waiting around for lorries, and being cold when it's windy and we can't lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, people can breathe, and I'd probably post a slightly sarcastic thing about all the panic. But I'd also say it already wiped out a lot of design work, so it's not nothing. Hype or not, my old clients stopped calling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'm already out of the field it hit, and nobody's sending a chat app up a ladder. I left design because a machine could draw a logo in four seconds, and it turns out it still can't fix a wall panel in the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep using AI every day like I do now, to read the drawings, check panel numbers, plan which order the lorries should unload. I'd finish my carpentry ticket and maybe ask to train on the crane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit like I bet on the right horse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the design work, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2024 my small studio lost about half its clients in a year. They'd make their own posters and logos with an app and come to us only to fix them, for a quarter of the price. I sold my share to my partner in the studio and took a few months to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why construction, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad was a builder, and I spent my childhood in his van. And factory-built houses felt like design you could stand inside. Tom, my husband, thought I'd lost my mind, he's a physiotherapist and he knows what this does to backs.

S0.say: I'd say people can breathe, maybe with a sarcastic post about the panic, but AI already wiped out lots of design work, so it wasn't nothing.
S0.think: She's fine, having already left the field AI hit; a machine can draw a logo in seconds but can't fix a wall panel in the wind.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily to read drawings, check panel numbers and plan lorry unloading. Finishes her carpentry ticket and asks to train on the crane.
S0.feel: Calm, like she bet on the right horse.
S0.quote: I left design because a machine could draw a logo in four seconds, and it turns out it still can't fix a wall panel in the wind.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha left graphic design after AI took half her studio's clients in 2024, so she's already lived one AI shock. She uses AI every day on site, which is unusual on her crew. Her father's building work drew her to the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it always goes: some tasks go, new ones appear, and the people who learn fast do fine. I'd say government should help with retraining and companies should pay for it too. I wouldn't make it political, it's just practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. Our crew is already half factory, half site, and the new jobs would be the ones linking the two. I'm already the one on site who talks to the computer, so this picture is basically my job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to train me on the crane and on whatever planning software comes in, in the first few months. I'd put a slice of savings, maybe ten percent, into shares in companies that make building robots, because if they win I'd rather win with them. I'd keep my carpentry going so I understand what the machines are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little buzzy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gav, who's been fixing panels for twenty years and still prints everything on paper. He's brilliant, he can feel when a panel is out by a few millimetres. I'd want him to teach the machines, or teach me, before somebody decides he's too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Investing in robot companies when they might replace your crew. Doesn't that feel strange?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I've watched this film before, in design. The people who owned the tools did well, and the people who sold the work by the hour didn't. I'd rather own a small piece than complain about it.

S1.say: I'd say tasks go, new ones appear, and fast learners do fine. Government and companies should both pay for retraining; it's practical, not political.
S1.think: She thinks it's good for her because she's already the one on site who talks to the computer. The new jobs linking factory and site suit her.
S1.do: Asks for crane and planning software training in the first months and puts about ten percent of savings into shares in building-robot companies. Keeps up her carpentry to understand what the machines do.
S1.quote: I'm already the one on site who talks to the computer, so this picture is basically my job description.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha sees steady disruption as matching what she already does. Her design years taught her that tool owners win, so she'd buy shares in robot makers despite the discomfort. She worries for Gav, a skilled veteran who still works on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need some sort of safety net quickly, because two years is no time for families. I'd say it calmly but clearly. I'd share practical stuff, like how to check your mortgage terms, rather than angry posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the one that gets me. I ran from AI once already. This is the one where there's nowhere left to run to. I'd be 45, and the thing I'm good at, learning fast, doesn't help if the machine learns faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd move a chunk of savings into paying down the mortgage and keep a year of bills in cash. I'd push more into shares in the robot and AI firms, because that's where the money goes. And I'd volunteer to run whatever machines the firm brings in, to stay useful as long as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops, because I know what that phone silence feels like when clients stop calling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Becoming the person who sets the robots up and checks them, as fast as possible. It might only buy me a year or two, but that's a year or two of wages. And getting the money arranged so the family's safe when the wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yuki and Sami?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yuki's twelve and draws all the time, like I did. I'd tell her to keep drawing because it's who she is, not because it'll be a job. Sami's nine, he'd ask if the robots can play football, and I'd say probably, love.

S2.say: I'd say we need a safety net quickly because two years is no time for families. I'd share practical tips, like checking mortgage terms, rather than angry posts.
S2.think: She ran from AI once and this is the picture with nowhere left to run. Her strength, learning fast, doesn't help if the machine learns faster.
S2.do: Moves savings into paying down the mortgage while keeping a year of bills in cash, and puts more into shares in robot and AI firms. Volunteers to run the firm's new machines to stay useful longer.
S2.feel: Anxious, with the familiar stomach-drop of clients going quiet.
S2.quote: I ran from AI once already. This is the one where there's nowhere left to run to.
S2.fieldNote: Even for someone adaptive, two years leaves Aisha with nowhere to run. She'd still try to be the one setting up the robots, knowing it buys only a year or two. Her advice to her daughter, to keep drawing for its own sake, reflects her own design story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if everyone gets moving, and I'd say get moving. Learn the tools, sort your money, don't wait. I'd probably bore people at parties with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years suits me better. I could get my ticket, get the crane qualification, and then learn the robot side properly. By 2031 I'd want to be the person the robots report to, not the person they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd sign up for a robotics or automation course at the college, evenings, while working. I'd keep investing a bit every month in robot and AI firms. Tom and I would also look at him moving into training other physios, because hands-on care might last longer but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but focused. I like having a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between surviving and choosing. With two years I'm grabbing whatever's nearest. With five, I can pick a lane and actually get good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'not forever' about Tom's job. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. He's always been the steady one, the job that would never go. If physio goes too, then it's both of us, and the savings start looking smaller. That's the bit I'd think about at night.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if everyone gets moving: learn the tools, sort your money and don't wait.
S3.think: She thinks five years suits her, time to get her ticket, the crane qualification and the robot skills. By 2031 she wants the robots to report to her rather than replace her.
S3.do: Takes an evening robotics or automation course in year one while working, and keeps investing monthly in robot and AI firms. Discusses with Tom moving into training other physiotherapists.
S3.feel: Uneasy but focused, enjoying having a project.
S3.quote: By 2031 I'd want to be the person the robots report to, not the person they replace.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Aisha choose a lane instead of grabbing the nearest thing. Her worry shifts to her husband's job, which she'd always seen as the safe one. She frames it all as a project, which steadies her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, and people should use it to retrain and plan. I'd say government should help, but don't wait for them. I'd be the annoying friend sending course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine with this one. Ten years is time to learn the trade, then the machines, then maybe start something that mixes design and building. People think I got out of design. Really I just moved it outdoors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my ticket and crane training in the first two years, then the robotics course. I'd start a small side business designing garden studios and having them built by the factory, using AI for the drawings. And I'd keep putting money into shares and the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan with enough room in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years gives the robots time too. Doesn't that make your side business riskier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, but people buying a garden studio want someone to talk to, someone who'll listen to their weird ideas about a reading nook. The AI can draw it, but I'm the one who asks the right questions. Clients never knew what they wanted until somebody sat in their kitchen and asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the decade that you'd dread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last couple of years, maybe, when it gets real and people around me start losing work. Gav, and the younger lads. Even if I'm fine, it'll be hard to watch.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a proper runway to retrain and plan. Government should help, but people shouldn't wait for them.
S4.think: She's fine with this one, with time to learn the trade, then the machines, then perhaps start a business mixing design and building. She never left design, she says, just moved it outdoors.
S4.do: Completes her ticket and crane training in two years, then a robotics course. Starts a side business designing garden studios built by the factory, and keeps investing in shares and her pension.
S4.feel: Calm, with a plan that has enough room in it.
S4.quote: Clients never knew what they wanted until somebody sat in their kitchen and asked.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Aisha builds a full plan combining design, building and robots. She believes listening to clients is what she adds over AI drawing. Her only dread is watching others, like Gav, lose work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's nowhere to run. What would help is a basic safety net that kicks in fast, and cheap evening courses for the robot side of building. And companies telling crews what's coming instead of just turning up with a machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd go back to design. I wouldn't. I miss it, but I don't miss waiting for the phone to ring. On site, at least the work turns up on a lorry.

headlineQuote: People think I got out of design. Really I just moved it outdoors.
portrait: Aisha Ito is a 43-year-old junior on a crew assembling factory-built timber houses, who spent eighteen years as a graphic designer until AI image tools took half her studio's clients. She sold her share, followed her builder father into the trade, and uses AI every day on site. She's practical and centrist, and she hedges by buying shares in robot firms because tool owners win. She's calm through the plateau and steady change, anxious at AGI in two years because she has nowhere left to run, and calmer with more time, planning crane, robotics and a garden studio side business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because after already running from AI once there would be nowhere left to run.
whatWouldHelp: A safety net that kicks in fast, cheap evening courses in the robot side of building, and companies telling crews what's coming.
